{"id": "b8798693-293c-4287-9dfb-8e40a9a89f27", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "tool_summary", "content": [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "tooluse_cGoOg5RJCdbPPfdz8407ZY", "status": "success", "content": [{"text": "{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"status\":\"SUCCESS\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/s3-data-source-connector.html\",\"content\":\"# Connect to Amazon S3 for your knowledge base\\n\\n**Important:**\\n\\nFor optimized retrieval accuracy and a managed experience, we recommend Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base.\\n\\nAmazon S3 is an object storage service that stores data as objects within buckets.\\nYou can connect to your Amazon S3 bucket for your Amazon Bedrock knowledge base by using either\\nthe AWS Management Console for Amazon Bedrock\\nor the CreateDataSource\\nAPI (see Amazon Bedrock supported SDKs and AWS CLI).\\n\\n**Multimodal content support:**\\n\\nAmazon S3 data sources support multimodal content including images, audio, and video files. For comprehensive guidance on working with multimodal content, see Build a knowledge base for multimodal content.\\n\\nYou can upload a small batch of files to an Amazon S3 bucket using the Amazon S3 console or API.\\nYou can alternatively use AWS DataSync to upload\\nmultiple files to S3 continuously, and transfer files on a schedule from on-premises, edge,\\nother cloud, or AWS storage.\\n\\nCurrently only General Purpose S3 buckets are supported.\\n\\nThere are limits to how many files and MB per file that can be crawled. See Quotas for knowledge bases.\\n\\n###### Topics\\n\\n* Supported features\\n* Prerequisites\\n* Connection configuration\\n\\n## Supported features\\n\\n* Document metadata fields\\n* Inclusion prefixes\\n* Incremental content syncs for added, updated, deleted content\\n\\n## Prerequisites\\n\\n**In Amazon S3, make sure you**:\\n\\n* Note the Amazon S3 bucket URI, Amazon Resource Name (ARN), and the AWS\\n  account ID for the owner of the bucket. You can find the URI and ARN\\n  in the properties section in the Amazon S3 console. Your bucket must be in the\\n  same Region as your Amazon Bedrock knowledge base. You must\\n  have permission to access the bucket.\\n\\n**In your AWS account, make sure you**:\\n\\n* Include the necessary permissions to connect to your data source in your\\n  AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role/permissions policy for your\\n  knowledge base. For information on the required permissions for this data source\\n  to add to your knowledge base IAM role, see\\n  Permissions to access data sources.\\n\\n**Note:**\\n\\nIf you use the console, the IAM role with all the required permissions\\ncan be created for you as part of the steps for creating a knowledge base. After\\nyou have configured your data source and other configurations, the IAM\\nrole with all the required permissions are applied to your specific knowledge base.\\n\\n## Connection configuration\\n\\nTo connect to your Amazon S3 bucket, you must provide the necessary configuration\\ninformation so that Amazon Bedrock can access and crawl your data. You must also follow the\\nPrerequisites.\\n\\nAn example of a configuration for this data source is included in this section.\\n\\nFor more information about inclusion filters,\\ndocument metadata fields, incremental syncing, and how these work, select\\nthe following:\\n\\n### Document metadata fields\\n\\nYou can include a separate file that specifies the document metadata fields/attributes for each\\nfile in your Amazon S3 data source and whether to include them in the embeddings when indexing the data source into the vector store. For example, you can\\ncreate a file in the following format, name it `fileName.extension.metadata.json` and upload it to your S3 bucket.\\n\\n```\\n\\n{\\n  \\\"metadataAttributes\\\": {\\n    \\\"company\\\": {\\n      \\\"value\\\": {\\n        \\\"type\\\": \\\"STRING\\\",\\n        \\\"stringValue\\\": \\\"BioPharm Innovations\\\"\\n      },\\n      \\\"includeForEmbedding\\\": true\\n    },\\n    \\\"created_date\\\": {\\n      \\\"value\\\": {\\n        \\\"type\\\": \\\"NUMBER\\\",\\n        \\\"numberValue\\\": 20221205\\n      },\\n      \\\"includeForEmbedding\\\": true\\n    },\\n    \\\"author\\\": {\\n      \\\"value\\\": {\\n        \\\"type\\\": \\\"STRING\\\",\\n        \\\"stringValue\\\": \\\"Lisa Thompson\\\"\\n      },\\n      \\\"includeForEmbedding\\\": true\\n    },\\n    \\\"origin\\\": {\\n      \\\"value\\\": {\\n        \\\"type\\\": \\\"STRING\\\",\\n        \\\"stringValue\\\": \\\"Overview\\\"\\n      },\\n      \\\"includeForEmbedding\\\": true\\n    }\\n  }\\n}\\n```\\n\\nThe metadata file must use the same name as its associated source document file,\\nwith `.metadata.json` appended onto the end of the file name. The metadata file\\nmust be stored in the same folder or location as the source file in your Amazon S3 bucket. The file\\nmust not exceed the limit of 10 KB. For information on the supported attribute/field data types\\nand the filtering operators you can apply to your metadata fields, see Metadata and filtering.\\n\\nThe `includeForEmbedding` field controls whether a metadata attribute is included when embedding the chunk:\\n\\n* `includeForEmbedding: false` \u2013 Only the chunk text is embedded and turned into a vector during ingestion. The metadata is still stored and available for filtering, but does not influence semantic search results.\\n* `includeForEmbedding: true` \u2013 The metadata key-value pair is concatenated to the chunk text before embedding (for example, `key1: value1\\\\n\\\\nchunk text`). This means the metadata information is included in the embedding vector, so queries mentioning the metadata key or value will contribute to the similarity score and boost search relevance. The metadata key-value pair is not included in the chunk text returned in results, ensuring that results contain only the raw content from source files.\\n\\nYou can also use a simplified format for metadata attributes when you don't need to control embedding behavior:\\n\\n```\\n{\\n    \\\"metadataAttributes\\\": {\\n        \\\"tag\\\": \\\"value\\\"\\n    }\\n}\\n```\\n\\nWith the simplified format, the metadata is stored for filtering but is not included in the embedding (equivalent to `includeForEmbedding: false`).\\n\\n### Inclusion prefixes\\n\\nYou can specify an inclusion prefix, which is an Amazon S3 path prefix, where you can use an S3 file\\nor a folder instead of the entire bucket to create the S3 data source connector.\\n\\n### Incremental syncing\\n\\nThe data source connector crawls new, modified, and deleted content each time your data\\nsource syncs with your knowledge base. Amazon Bedrock can use your data source\u2019s mechanism\\nfor tracking content changes and crawl content that changed since the last sync. When you sync\\nyour data source with your knowledge base for the first time, all content is crawled by default.\\n\\nTo sync your data source with your knowledge base, use the StartIngestionJob\\nAPI or select your knowledge base in the console and select **Sync** within the\\ndata source overview section.\\n\\n**Important:**\\n\\nAll data that you sync from your data source becomes available to anyone with\\n`bedrock:Retrieve` permissions to retrieve the data. This can also include any\\ndata with controlled data source permissions. For more\\ninformation, see Knowledge base permissions.\\n\\n#### Using Console\\n\\n###### To connect an Amazon S3 bucket to your knowledge base\\n\\n1. Follow the steps at Create a knowledge base by connecting to a data source in Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases and choose **Amazon S3** as the data source.\\n2. Provide a name for the data source.\\n3. {"id": "741035cf-4789-4edc-a1d1-59dfd8442387", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "A sync can finish successfully and still index nothing, because the job only processes files that match the data source's S3 settings. The documentation covers some of these causes directly. The rest come from how the connector behaves.

**Most likely causes, roughly in order**

1. **Inclusion prefix doesn't match the file location.**
   - The data source only crawls keys under its configured `inclusionPrefixes`. A prefix of `documents` or `/documents/` won't match the same files as `documents/`.
   - Check for a leading slash, a case mismatch, or a prefix that is one level too deep or too shallow. S3 prefixes are literal, case-sensitive string matches.
   - Also confirm the data source points at the bucket you think it does.

2. **Wrong bucket, account or Region.**
   - The bucket must be a general purpose bucket in the same Region as the knowledge base.
   - If the bucket is in another account, the `bucketOwnerAccountId` on the data source has to be correct.

3. **Unsupported file types or empty files.**
   - Only the documented formats and sizes are ingested. Other files, such as extensionless objects, are skipped rather than failing the job.
   - Objects that are "folder" placeholders (keys ending in `/`) or zero-byte files also contribute nothing.

4. **Files were already indexed, or the files are new but the sync was triggered too early.**
   - Syncs are incremental. A later sync only processes added, changed or deleted content. If you uploaded after the job started, or the objects were already counted in a prior run, the job can report zero new documents.

5. **Permissions on the knowledge base service role.**
   - The role needs `s3:ListBucket` and `s3:GetObject` on the bucket and prefix. It also needs `kms:Decrypt` if the bucket uses a customer-managed KMS key.
   - If the role can't list the prefix, it's possible the crawl sees no objects instead of raising an error. I haven't confirmed that behavior in the docs, so treat it as a check, not a certainty.

6. **Metadata files mistaken for content.**
   - Files named `<file>.metadata.json` are treated as metadata for a source file. If the prefix holds only metadata files, or the source files they refer to are missing, nothing is indexed.

**Quick way to narrow it down**
- Look at the ingestion job's statistics: scanned, indexed, failed and skipped counts. If scanned is 0, the cause is the prefix, bucket or permissions (causes 1, 2 and 5). If scanned is above 0 but indexed is 0, it's file type, size or parsing (causes 3 and 6).
- Check the job's failure reasons, and turn on knowledge base logging to CloudWatch if it isn't already enabled.

If you give me the knowledge base ID and data source ID, I can read the data source config, the latest ingestion job statistics, and the S3 prefix contents. I can also check the service role's S3 permissions, and tell you which of these applies. I'd need the Region and account as well if it isn't in the one this space covers (us-east-1, 012345678901_1).", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}

1. **Inclusion prefix doesn't match the file location.**
   - The data source only crawls keys under its configured `inclusionPrefixes`. A prefix of `documents` or `/documents/` won't match the same files as `documents/`.
   - Check for a leading slash, a case mismatch, or a prefix that is one level too deep or too shallow. S3 prefixes are literal, case-sensitive string matches.
   - Also confirm the data source points at the bucket you think it does.

2. **Wrong bucket, account or Region.**
   - The bucket must be a general purpose bucket in the same Region as the knowledge base.
   - If the bucket is in another account, the `bucketOwnerAccountId` on the data source has to be correct.

3. **Unsupported file types or empty files.**
   - Only the documented formats and sizes are ingested. Other files, such as extensionless objects, are skipped rather than failing the job.
   - Objects that are "folder" placeholders (keys ending in `/`) or zero-byte files also contribute nothing.

4. **Files were already indexed, or the files are new but the sync was triggered too early.**
   - Syncs are incremental. A later sync only processes added, changed or deleted content. If you uploaded after the job started, or the objects were already counted in a prior run, the job can report zero new documents.

5. **Permissions on the knowledge base service role.**
   - The role needs `s3:ListBucket` and `s3:GetObject` on the bucket and prefix. It also needs `kms:Decrypt` if the bucket uses a customer-managed KMS key.
   - If the role can't list the prefix, it's possible the crawl sees no objects instead of raising an error. I haven't confirmed that behavior in the docs, so treat it as a check, not a certainty.

6. **Metadata files mistaken for content.**
   - Files named `<file>.metadata.json` are treated as metadata for a source file. If the prefix holds only metadata files, or the source files they refer to are missing, nothing is indexed.

**Quick way to narrow it down**
- Look at the ingestion job's statistics: scanned, indexed, failed and skipped counts. If scanned is 0, the cause is the prefix, bucket or permissions (causes 1, 2 and 5). If scanned is above 0 but indexed is 0, it's file type, size or parsing (causes 3 and 6).
- Check the job's failure reasons, and turn on knowledge base logging to CloudWatch if it isn't already enabled.
